clinicalPearls: CML is a clonal hematopoietic myeloproliferative stem cell neoplasm driven by the BCR::ABL1 chimeric gene, which encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase (Harrison 22e p.834).

BCR::ABL1 results from a balanced reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22, t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2), known as the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph); the t(9;22) is present in >90% of classical CML cases (Harrison 22e p.834-835).

The most common transcript in CML encodes the p210BCR::ABL1 oncoprotein; p190BCR::ABL1 is present in two-thirds of Ph-positive ALL but rare in CML, and p230BCR::ABL1 is rare and associated with a more indolent course (Harrison 22e p.835).
Untreated, CML is typically biphasic or triphasic: an early indolent chronic phase, often followed by an accelerated phase, and a terminal blastic phase (Harrison 22e p.834).
Most patients (about 90%) present in chronic phase; in developed countries 50-60% are diagnosed on routine blood tests with minimal symptoms such as fatigue (Harrison 22e p.836).
Common symptoms, when present, are manifestations of anemia and splenomegaly: fatigue, malaise, weight loss, early satiety, and left upper quadrant pain or mass (Harrison 22e p.836).
Splenomegaly is the most common physical finding (20-70% depending on screening frequency); hepatomegaly (5-10%) and lymphadenopathy (5%) are less common (Harrison 22e p.836-837).

Untreated CML shows leukocytosis (10-500 x 10^9/L) with left-shifted myeloid hematopoiesis: neutrophils plus bands, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, promyelocytes, and blasts (usually <=5%); basophils and/or eosinophils are frequently increased (Harrison 22e p.837).

Thrombocytosis is common; thrombocytopenia is rare and, when present, suggests worse prognosis, disease acceleration, or an unrelated etiology. Anemia is present in one-third of patients (Harrison 22e p.837).

Diagnosis depends on documenting t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2), identified by G-banding in 90% of cases; FISH and PCR aid diagnosis and estimate disease burden, and can be done on peripheral blood (Harrison 22e p.837).

TKIs have revolutionized CML: the estimated 10-year survival with imatinib now exceeds 85% and approaches that of a normal age-matched population; allogeneic HSCT (curative but riskier) is offered as later-line therapy after TKI failure (Harrison 22e p.834).

Molecular monitoring on the International Scale (IS) guides therapy: complete cytogenetic response (0% Ph) is roughly equivalent to BCR::ABL1 <=1% (MR2); major molecular response (MMR/MR3) is BCR::ABL1 <=0.1%; deep molecular response MR4 is <=0.01% and MR4.5 is <=0.0032% (Harrison 22e p.837-838).

The T315I 'gatekeeper' kinase-domain mutation prevents binding of, and causes resistance to, imatinib and the second-generation TKIs (dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib); third-generation agents (e.g., ponatinib, asciminib) retain activity against it (Harrison 22e p.836).
harrison.pathophysiology: CML is a clonal myeloproliferative stem cell neoplasm caused by the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene arising from the reciprocal balanced translocation t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2) (the Philadelphia chromosome). DNA from the ABL1 proto-oncogene on chromosome 9 is juxtaposed to the breakpoint cluster region (BCR) gene on chromosome 22, generating a hybrid oncogene whose product (most commonly the p210BCR::ABL1 oncoprotein from e13a2 or e14a2 transcripts) has constitutive tyrosine kinase activity. This drives increased proliferation and reduced apoptosis, giving CML cells a growth advantage and progressively suppressing normal hematopoiesis. Constitutive BCR::ABL1 activation triggers autophosphorylation and downstream signaling via RAS, MAP kinases, STAT, PI3K, MYC and others, mediated by adapter proteins (GRB-2, CRK, CRK-L, SHC). Most TKIs bind the ATP-binding domain to inhibit kinase activity; asciminib (a STAMP inhibitor) instead binds the ABL1 myristoyl pocket. BCR::ABL1 induces genetic instability favoring acquisition of additional defects (e.g., double Ph, trisomy 8, isochromosome 17/17p loss of TP53, 3q26 abnormalities, mutations in TP53, RB1, RUNX1, p16) that drive transformation from chronic to accelerated to blastic phase. Notably, the BCR::ABL1 rearrangement is detectable in the blood of up to 25% of normal adults and 5% of infants but is not sufficient to cause overt CML in the overwhelming majority. (Harrison 22e p.834-836)
additionalDifferentials: Leukemoid reaction (reactive leukocytosis) - distinguished from CML by a high/normal leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score (CML has a LOW LAP) and absence of BCR::ABL1 (Harrison 22e p.837)

Atypical CML (BCR::ABL1-negative) - lacks the Ph chromosome/BCR::ABL1, does not respond to TKI therapy, associated with SETBP1 (about 25%) and some CSF3R mutations, poor prognosis with median survival ~2-3 years (Harrison 22e p.835)
Chronic neutrophilic leukemia - frequently CSF3R-mutated (about 80%); may respond to ruxolitinib (Harrison 22e p.835)
Myelodysplastic syndrome/myeloproliferative neoplasms, including MDS/MPN-RS-T (SF3B1-mutated) (Harrison 22e p.835)
Essential thrombocythemia and other Ph-negative MPNs presenting with thrombocytosis - when JAK2 V617F is absent, cytogenetics/FISH for BCR::ABL1 are required to exclude CML (Harrison 22e p.832-833)
nonInfectiousMimics: Leukemoid reaction (reactive leukocytosis from infection, inflammation, or other stress) - mimics the leukocytosis with left shift of CML but lacks BCR::ABL1 and shows a high/normal (not low) leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score (Harrison 22e p.837)
Other myeloproliferative neoplasms and MDS/MPN overlap syndromes that can produce leukocytosis, basophilia, or splenomegaly without the Philadelphia chromosome (Harrison 22e p.835)
additionalInvestigations: Bone marrow aspiration with routine G-banding cytogenetics - required to confirm the Ph chromosome, detect additional chromosomal abnormalities (which FISH will not detect), and quantify marrow blasts and basophils; a diagnosis of CML must always rely on marrow analysis with cytogenetics (Harrison 22e p.837)
FISH analysis for BCR::ABL1 on peripheral blood - quantifies percentage of Ph-positive cells; preferred when a Ph cytogenetic study is negative or for monitoring (Harrison 22e p.837)

Quantitative RT-PCR for BCR::ABL1 transcripts on the International Scale - baseline transcript typing at diagnosis (to avoid spurious 'undetectable' results on follow-up with atypical transcripts) and serial molecular monitoring of response (Harrison 22e p.837-838)
ABL1 kinase domain mutation analysis - assessed when resistance/loss of response is suspected (e.g., to detect T315I) (Harrison 22e p.836-837)
Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score - characteristically LOW in CML, helping distinguish it from a leukemoid reaction (Harrison 22e p.837)
Supportive biochemistry - high vitamin B12, uric acid, lactate dehydrogenase, and lysozyme are commonly seen (Harrison 22e p.837)
redFlags: Unexplained, sustained leukocytosis (with or without splenomegaly) should prompt marrow examination and cytogenetic analysis (Harrison 22e p.837)
Increasing/therapy-resistant leukocytosis, worsening anemia, fever and constitutional symptoms, and rising blasts and basophils signal disease progression (Harrison 22e p.838)
New thrombocytopenia (<100 x 10^9/L unrelated to therapy) suggests worse prognosis or disease acceleration (Harrison 22e p.837-838)
Extramedullary disease (skin/subcutaneous lesions, soft tissue, or lytic bone lesions) with biopsy showing blast predominance indicates transformation (Harrison 22e p.837-838)
Hyperleukocytosis/hyperviscosity or marked thrombocytosis with thrombotic events (priapism, MI, venous thrombosis, visual disturbance, CVA) or bleeding diathesis (Harrison 22e p.836)
harrison.prognosis: TKIs have transformed CML prognosis. Before the TKI era median survival was 3-7 years with annual mortality of 10% in the first 2 years and 15-20% thereafter. With imatinib, annual mortality has fallen to about 1-2%, the 10-year survival rate is about 85% (CML-specific survival ~90%), and the 10-year incidence of blastic transformation is only 5-6%; more than half of deaths are now from non-CML causes. Treatment-related response milestones are the dominant modern prognostic factors: achievement of complete cytogenetic response (MR2) is the major endpoint associated with improved survival, while durable deep molecular response (MR4/MR4.5) may permit treatment-free remission (TFR rate about 50% after 2+ years of durable DMR and 80%+ after 5+ years). Historical pretreatment models (Sokal, Hasford, EUTOS) and adverse features (age, splenomegaly, anemia, high blasts/basophils, marrow fibrosis, additional chromosomal abnormalities) have lost much of their prognostic weight in the TKI era. Accelerated phase (historical median survival <2 years) and blastic phase carry the worst outcomes; de novo accelerated phase on TKI now has an estimated 8-year survival of 60-70%, and lymphoid blastic phase responds to ALL-type chemotherapy plus TKIs (complete response ~70%, median survival ~3 years). (Harrison 22e p.834, 838-839)
pitfalls: PITFALL: Mistaking a reactive leukemoid reaction for CML - the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score is LOW in CML but high/normal in a leukemoid reaction, and CML requires demonstration of BCR::ABL1 (Harrison 22e p.837).

Atypical transcripts (e13a3, e14a3, e19a2, etc.) not detected at diagnosis can produce falsely 'negative/undetectable' BCR::ABL1 on follow-up PCR, giving a false impression of complete molecular response; transcript type must be documented at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.835, 837).
FISH does NOT detect additional chromosomal abnormalities, so a marrow cytogenetic analysis is still required at diagnosis; relying on FISH/PCR alone can miss clonal evolution (Harrison 22e p.837).
Both FISH and PCR can be falsely positive at low levels or falsely negative for technical reasons, so diagnosis must always rely on marrow analysis with routine cytogenetics (Harrison 22e p.837).

In about 10% of patients marrow blasts and basophils are significantly higher than in peripheral blood, conferring poorer prognosis or representing transformation that peripheral counts alone would miss (Harrison 22e p.837).
Failure to achieve MMR or DMR should NOT automatically be considered 'failure' of a given TKI or an indication to switch TKI or proceed to allogeneic HSCT (Harrison 22e p.838).
harrison.severityClassification: CML is staged by clinical phase. Chronic phase: indolent, marrow blasts typically <=5%, where ~90% of patients present. Accelerated phase (historically median survival <2 years): >=15% peripheral blasts, >=30% peripheral blasts plus promyelocytes, >=20% peripheral basophils, cytogenetic clonal evolution (additional chromosomal abnormalities beyond Ph), or thrombocytopenia <100 x 10^9/L unrelated to therapy. Blastic phase: >=30% peripheral or marrow blasts, or sheets of blasts in extramedullary disease (commonly myeloid in ~60%, lymphoid in ~25%). The newest WHO classification suggests eliminating accelerated phase and reclassifying such patients as high-risk CML, but the text argues the accelerated-phase definition should be maintained because their survival is significantly worse than high-risk CML. Risk models (Sokal, Hasford, EUTOS) were used historically. (Harrison 22e p.838)
